As a younger <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, that son was originally intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and went at an early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Scotland, in 1750, to enter as a student in the university of Glasgow, so that he was initiated almost in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of Grecian literature under the able instruction of Dr Moor, the well-known professor of Greek; and he acquired such a knowledge of the classical languages as served to constitute him a correct scholar through <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He pursued his studies with so much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> as to obtain the approbation of his teachers and the admiration of his contemporaries, who were delighted with the originality and ingenuity of his conversation, though he did not himself reflect with perfect satisfaction upon the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of application which he had exerted in his academical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. He took the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts in 1756, having studied <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> under Dr Robert Simson, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> under Dr <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Smith. The example of so correct and rigid a follower of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> methods of demonstration as Dr Simson, must unquestionably have exercised considerable influence on his yet unformed <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in mathematics; but he seems to have had a natural preference, either from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of his mind, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> from some previously acquired habits of thinking, for the geometrical method; for we are informed that "he first attracted the regard of Dr Simson by owning his dislike of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, and by returning a neat geometrical solution of a problem which had been given out to the class in an algebraical form: with this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of solution the professor was delighted, though the pupil candidly acknowledged that it had been adopted only because he could not solve the problem in the manner required of the class." In the course of his studies, he had imbibed an insuperable aversion to the pursuit of his original objects in the church; not certainly from any want of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> feeling, or from a dislike to the kind of life that was intended for him, but probably from some difficulties that had occurred to him respecting particular <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of doctrine or of practice. He was therefore compelled to provide himself with some other occupation; and he readily accepted the offer of some of his friends in 1758, to recommend him to Dr Blair, a prebendary of Westminster, who had formed a scheme for sending <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward, the young <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>, to complete his professional education at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in com- pany with a son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Knowles; and Mr Robison was to have instructed his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness in mathematics and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. On his arrival in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he was much disappointed to find that the expedition had never been seriously intended; and he readily accepted an engagement to attend young Knowles as a private <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, when he went as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MIDSHIPMAN">midshipman</a> on board of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> of ninety guns, with Admiral Saunders, who had the command of a force intended to co-operate with General Wolfe in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Quebec; and upon the appointment of his friend as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> on board of the Royal William, Robison was himself rated as a midshipman in that ship. The fleet arrived on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in April 1759; in May they got up the river, and Mr Robison was one of a party of 100 seamen draughted from the Royal William into the admiral's ship, under the command of Lieutenant Knowles. In this capacity he had an opportunity of seeing considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and of making some surveys of the river and of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; an employment for which he was perfectly qualified, both as a geometrician and a draughtsman. He also remarked the effect of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol4.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis on the compass, which had been noticed by Mairan and Wargentin some years before, but which was then not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known. After the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> which was signalized by the victory and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the gallant Wolfe, the Royal William sailed with his body to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and arrived at Spithead in November. The next year she was sent to cruise off <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>; but in six months she was obliged to return home, from having the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the men disabled by the scurvy. He used to consider the two years that he spent on board of the Royal William as the happiest of his life; and no considerable part of his gratification was derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEAMANSHIP">seamanship</a> as he <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it practised under the auspices of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Hugh Pigot. He did not, however, acquire any firm <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the mode of life which he had temporarily adopted; he was rather disposed to resume his academical pursuits, and he had overcome his earlier objections to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession. He could not, however, refuse the kindly invitation of Admiral Knowles to come and live with him in the country, and to assist him in some important experiments which he was making upon <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> and nautical subjects. In the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February 1762, Lieutenant Knowles was appointed to the Peregrine sloop, of twenty guns, and Mr Robison accompanied him with the hope of becoming a purser. He visited <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> and several other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; but he found a cruise in a small ship much less convenient and agreeable than in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one; and, fortunately for himself and for mankind, he finally quitted the Peregrine and the naval service in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and returned to live with Admiral Knowles, who soon after recommended him as a proper person to take <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of Harrison's timekeeper, which had been completed by the labour of thirty-five years, after many unsuccessful experiments, and which was now sent out by desire of the Board of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a> to the West Indies, under the care of young Harrison and of Mr Robison. The rate of the chronometer was ascertained at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> the 6th November 1762, and it indicated at Port Royal, in Jamaica, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> amounting to $5^{\circ} 2^{\prime\prime} 47^{\prime\prime}$, which is only four seconds less than the true longitude. After a few days the observers had a prompt opportunity of returning home by the Merlin sloop, which was sent to Europe with despatches. The voyage was most disastrous with respect to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and at last the ship took fire; but she arrived safe at Portsmouth in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and on the 3rd of April the watch gave $11^{\text{h}} 58^{\text{m}} 63^{\text{s}}$, instead of $12^{\text{h}}$, for the time of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> noon, so that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, after six months, was only $1^{\text{h}} 53^{\text{m}} 43^{\text{s}}$, amounting to no more than about twenty miles of distance. Mr Robison received, upon his return, the afflicting intelligence of the total loss of the Peregrine, which had founded at sea with her commander and the whole of the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. He was also greatly disappointed in the failure of some hopes which had been held out to him from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">Admiralty</a> and the Board of Longitude; though in fact there is little reason for the public to regret that he was not gratified with the pursership, which he claimed as the reward of his services. He was indeed afterwards actually made a purser by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, in 1763; but he then declined accepting the appointment. His biographers very naturally complain of the neglect of those boards which ought to have recompensed him; but certainly the Board of Longitude had no power whatever, and probably not much influence, in the appointment of a purser; and, after all, the delay of a year or two was nothing very uncommon in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. He had now no other resource than to return to Glasgow, and to resume his academical pursuits with renewed energy. It was from this time that he dated his serious application to his studies. He became extremely intimate with Dr Reid and Dr Alexander Wilson; and he had the advantage of being a witness of two of the greatest steps in the improvement of physical science that have been made in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>'s experimental <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and Mr Watt's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine. Dr Black was the first that determined the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of heat required for the conversion of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>: Mr Watt, who was settled as a mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>-maker at Glasgow, had been employed in repairing a working <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of Newcomen's engine for one of the professors of the university; and it was the difficulty of supplying this model with steam that suggested to Mr Watt the eligibility of having a separate condenser, and that led him, in conjunction with Dr Black, to a knowledge of the quantity of heat consumed in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>. Amid the enthusiasm which is always inspired by the progress of scientific discovery and of practical improvement, Mr Robison found every encouragement and every facility for the pursuit of his favourite objects. He was recommended by Dr Black, upon his removal to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1766, as his successor in the lectureship of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, though without the appointment of a professor. He took charge, also, of the education of Mr Macdowall of Garthland, and of Mr <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Knowles, afterwards Sir Charles. Admiral Knowles was soon after recommended by the British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the empress of Russia, in order to effect a reformation in her navy, having been employed on a similar service in Portugal almost fifty years before; he had always been a firm friend to Mr Robison, and now engaged him on this mission, with a salary of L250 a year; and they proceeded together to St Petersburg in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1770. Being hospitably entertained on their way by the prince bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, whom they found to constitute, with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> and all his servants, a lodge of freemasons, Mr Robison was easily persuaded to become one of that fraternity: in a few days he was made an apprentice, and by degrees attained the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of Scottish master, as he has himself related in his publication upon the subject. He <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> nearly two years at St Petersburg, still acting in the capacity of private secretary to Sir Charles, who was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Board of Admiralty, much to the advantage of the Russian navy, though his improvements were frequently retarded by the prejudices of the native officers. Mr Robison was then appointed inspector general of the corps of marine cadets at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> salary, and with the rank of lieutenant-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>. His duty was to receive the report of about forty teachers and professors, respecting the studies of 400 young noblemen, who were their pupils, and to class them according to his judgment of their merits; but he had himself nothing to teach, nor could he have had much occasion for "lecturing fluently..." in the Russian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>," though he was introduced by his friend Kutusoff to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Duke Paul as a proficient in that language; but to the empress he was not personally known. At Petersburg he could have lived without regretting his country, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of such men as Euler and Alpinus, admired by the Russians, and beloved by the British; but Cronstadt in winter was deplorably melancholy; and in 1773 he was induced, without much difficulty, to make some little pecuniary sacrifice in accepting the professorship of natural philosophy at Edinburgh, which had become vacant by the death of Dr Russell, and to which he had been recommended by Dr Robertson, then <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the university. His determination was not disapproved by the Russian government, who granted him a pension of about L80 a year for life; but it was only paid as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> as three or four young men, who had accompanied him as pupils, continued to reside at Edinburgh; some discontent having been expressed because he did not keep up a correspondence with the academy on the improvement of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> education. He arrived at Edinburgh in September 1774. He married soon afterwards, and continued to reside in that city for the remaining thirty years of his life, paying only an annual visit to his native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where he possessed a part of the paternal estate; not being solicitous to extend it, although "he did not diminish it otherwise than as it had been diminished before," that is, in making provision for younger children. His predecessor had been very judicious and successful as a lecturer, though not a mathematician of the highest order: he had himself more practical knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and was better acquainted with the foreign mathematicians, who had naturally fallen under his notice during his residence on the continent. His lectures were considered by most of his pupils as somewhat too difficult to be followed; a complaint which, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did not depend on their own want of preparatory information, arose perhaps rather more from the hasty manner of his enunciation than from the abstruseness of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. "The singular facility of his own <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>," says Professor Playfair, "made him judge too favourably of the same power in others. To understand his lectures completely was, on account of the rapidity and the uniform flow of his discourse, not a very easy task, even for men tolerably familiar with the subject. On this account his lectures were less popular than might have been expected from such a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of talents as the author of them possessed." This inconvenience was increased by the small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments he introduced, and a view that he took of natural philosophy, which left but a very subordinate place for them to occupy. An experiment, he would very truly observe, does not establish a general proposition, and never can do more than prove a particular fact;" but he seems to have carried this principle to some little excess: it is, in fact, the illustration, and not the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, of general principles that is the object of a public <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of experiments; and it is very doubtful whether <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>, or Newton, or Leibnitz, or Euler, would have been very successful as showmen. With respect, however, to "accuracy of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, to clearness, brevity, and elegance of demonstration, and even to neatness and precision in experiments," Professor Robison was very successful; his course extended "to every branch of physics and of mixed mathematics," and entered so fully into the detail of each particular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the subjects, that "a more perfect system of academical instruction is not easily to be imagined." Nothing, in short, was wanting, but so much previous knowledge of mathematics in his pupils as he thought he had a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to expect, though his expectations were too rarely fulfilled. The Philosophical Society of Edinburgh had almost been suffered to sink into oblivion after the publication of the third volume of its Essays, in 1756. Professor Robison became a member of it soon after his return from Russia, and was chosen secretary of the new society upon its formation by royal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> in 1783, when it incorporated with itself the whole of the surviving members of the former society. In 1798 he received the compliment of a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Laws from the university of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>; and a similar <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> was paid him at Glasgow the year after. In 1800 he was elected, as successor to Dr Black, on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the foreign members of the Royal Academy of Sciences of St Petersburg. In 1785 he was attacked by a severe disorder, from which he was never afterwards wholly free, though it produced little inconvenience besides pain, with some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits, which was, however, attributed rather to the closeness of his application than to the immediate effect of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which was a glandular induration. For many years he was obliged to obtain the assistance of substitutes in the delivery of his lectures; but towards the end of his life he was able again to perform the duties of the professorship in person. He continued his literary labours with little intermission, and was most happy in the care and attention of his wife and children, whose virtues he found the best alleviation of his sufferings. He took a slight <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, after giving a lecture, on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1805, and died on the 30th. 1. It was comparatively late in life that Professor Robison assumed the character of an author, having communicated to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, in 1786, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the Determination of the Orbit and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a> of the Georium Sidus, which was published in the Edinburgh Transactions, vol. I. He had observed the opposition of the planet with an equatorial <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> only, and he had computed the elements of its orbit with greater accuracy than any other astronomer had then done; although his suspicion of the effect of such a planet on the motions of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> has not been confirmed by later investigations, the irregularities of these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, on the contrary, having been otherwise explained. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> paper, published in the same collection, vol. ii. p. 82, relates to the Motion of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, as affected by refracting or reflecting substances which are themselves in motion. The author corrects some errors of Boscovich, who had miscalculated the effect of a water-telescope; but he seems to agree with Dr Wilson in the suggestion of another experiment of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which, to say the least, is wholly superfluous. 3. The most important, beyond all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, of Professor Robison's scientific publications, are the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> which he communicated from time to time to the third edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, and to its Supplement. It was under the care of Mr Colin Macfarquhar that the first twelve volumes of that edition of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> were published; and upon his death, in 1793, the task of continuing it was committed to Dr Gleig, to whom Professor Robison became a most essential co-operator, and from that time "the work ceased to be a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> compilation." The first of his contributions, according to Professor Playfair, was the article <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, but it is probable he only revised and enlarged that article: it was followed by Philosophy, which he wrote jointly with Dr Gleig; by Physics, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>, Precession, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROJECTILES">Projectiles</a>, Pumps, Resistance, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">Roof</a>, Rope-making, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-ROTATION">Rotation</a>, Seamanship, Signal, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, Specific Gravity, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STATICS">Statics</a>, Steam, Steam-Engine, Steelyard, Strength, Telescope, Tide, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">Variation</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS">Water-works</a>; and in the --- 1 The third edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica consisted of eighteen volumes; the Supplement to it of two volumes. Robison. Supplement, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCH">Arch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, Boscovich, Carpen- try, Centre, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DYNAMICS">Dynamics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, Impulsion, In- volution, Machinery, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a>, Mechanics, Per- cussion, Pianoforte, Position, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">Temperament</a>, Thun- der, Trumpet, Tschirnhaus, and Watch-work. Not- withstanding some degree of prolixity and want of arrange- ment, which could scarcely be avoided in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of original articles for such a mode of publication, the whole of them, taken together, undeniably exhibit a more com- plete view of the modern improvements of physical science than had ever before been in the possession of the British public; and display such a combination of acquired know- ledge with original power of reasoning, as has fallen to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of a few only of the most favoured of mankind. 4. It is not altogether with so <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> approbation that his friends and his biographers have mentioned a work, of a nature rather <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> than philosophical, entitled Proofs of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">Conspiracy</a> against all the Religions and Governments of Europe, Edinb. 1797, 8vo; though it went through several editions. The principal part of the book consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ILLUMINATI">Illuminati</a> and the German Union, whom he considers as having become the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> agents in a plot first formed by the freemasons, at the suggestion of some ex- jesuit, who proposed for their model the internal economy of the order which he had quitted; and whatever founda- tion this outline may have had in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, there is no doubt that the manner in which Professor Robison has filled it up, betrays a degree of credulity extremely remarkable in a person used to calm reasoning and philosophical demon- stration: for example, in the admission of a story told by an anonymous German author, that the minister Turgot was the protector of a society that met at Baron d'Hol- bach's, for the purpose of examining the brains of living children, in order to discover the principle of vitality. He does not accuse the English freemasons of having partici- pated in the conspiracy; but he considers the continental lodges as having been universally implicated in it. 5. After the death of Dr Black, in 1799, he undertook to superintend the publication of his Lectures on Chemistry, which appeared in 1803, 2 vols. 4to. And this task, which was rather laborious than difficult, he executed with equal zeal and ability. He endeavoured to reduce to their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> estimate the comparative pretensions of the French and British chemists, though he is somewhat puritanically se- vere in criticizing the literal meaning of the compliments paid to Black by Lavoisier, on which he finds a charge of insincerity. 6. His last publication was the first volume of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> which was to form a complete system, entitled Elements of Mechanical Philosophy, Edinb. 1804, 8vo. It comprehended only Dynamics and Astronomy, and it never became very popular; it was too difficult for the many, who wished for general and philosophical notions only, and not sufficiently precise and demonstrative for the few, who wanted practi- cal and numerical results. In attempting to combine the separate merits of the Exposition du Système du Monde, and of the Mécanique Céleste, the author sacrificed both the popular simplicity of the former, and the mathematical perfection of the latter. A few inaccuracies, which ought not to escape the attention of the reader of the work, have been pointed out in the Imperial Review for March 1805; a journal long since discontinued. 7. The contents of the volume last mentioned, together with some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> intended to have formed part of a second, and the greater part of the articles furnished by Professor Robison to the Encyclopaedia, were collected into a System of Mechanical Philosophy, with Notes, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Brewster, LL.D. Edinb. 1822, 4 vols. 8vo; a spirit- ed bookseller in London having undertaken the risk of the publication. 1. The first volume begins with the articles Dynamics, Projectiles, Corpuscular Forces, Capil- lary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRACTION">Attraction</a>, Boscovich's Theory, and Rotation, Robi- son as remodelled for the Elements; then follow Strength of Materials, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARPENTRY">Carpentry</a>, Roof, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">Arches</a>, Construction of Centres. 2. The article Steam-Engine is enriched with notes and an appendix by the late Mr Watt: the next is Machinery, then Re- sistance of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, Rivers, Water-works, Pumps. 3. Astronomy, Telescope, Pneumatics. 4. Electrici- ty, Magnetism, Variation, Temperament, Trumpet, Watch-work, and Seamanship. The notes are not nu- merous, and the editor's principal labour has been to re- trench some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> that appeared to him superfluous when the papers were to stand as parts of such a collection. "Although Dr Robison's name," says Dr Brewster in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, "cannot be associated with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> discoveries of the century which he adorned, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his talents and his virtues <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be long cherished by his coun- try. Imbued with the genuine spirit of the philosophy which he taught, he was one of the warmest patrons of ge- nius wherever it was found. His mind was nobly elevated above the mean jealousies of rival ambition, and his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of science and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was too ardent to allow him either to depreciate the labours of others, or to transfer them to himself. To these great qualities as a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, Dr Ro- bison added all the more estimable endowments of domes- tic and of social life. His friendship was at all times ge- nerous and sincere. His piety was ardent and unosten- tious. His <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> was of the most pure and exalted character; and, like the immortal Newton, whose memory he cherished with a peculiar reverence, he was pre-em- inently entitled to the high distinction of a Christian, patriot, and philosopher." His person was handsome, and his phy- siognomy prepossessing; and he appears to have been en- dowed with an extraordinary combination of talents, even exclusively of those which were called into immediate ac- tivity in his professional pursuits; for he was a good lin- guist, an excellent draughtsman, and an accomplished mu- sician. His conversation was always energetic and inter- esting, and sometimes even poetical; and his liberality of sentiment was only limited by his regard for what he con- sidered as the best interests of mankind. A short account of his life was published in 1802, by a contributor to the Philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, who, among other inaccuracies, thought himself at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to assert that he was an admirer of the algebraical form of representation, in preference to the geometrical. His friend Dr Gieg soon after stepped forward to correct these mistakes, in the Antijacobin Review for 1802, and his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was copied into the Philosophical Magazine. He asserts, from his own knowledge, that even yet Professor Robison "delights much more in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> than in any of the modes of alge- bra, assigning as the reason of his preference, that in the longest demonstration the geometrician has always clear and adequate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, which the most expert algebraist can very seldom have." It may perhaps be asserted, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that the same reasoning would <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us always to employ actual multiplication or division, in preference to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> or of a sliding rule; and that the whole of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> of calculation depends on the abstrac- tion of the results from the numerous and separately unim- portant steps by which they are obtained; but the having once seen those steps clearly is certainly of great impor- tance to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of reasoning, even when the memory no longer retains them; and no mathematician of correct taste can study the ancient geometricians without admiring the elegance and precision of their method, even amidst the pedantry which too frequently envelopes their expressions, and without being grateful for their punctuality in collect- ing their results into the very convenient form of distinct <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, and in making such references from each pro- position to the foundations on which it depends, as to es- able him readily to trace back their steps to the most elementary principles; which is scarcely possible in any of the works of the most modern school of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>. Professor Robison, however, seems rarely to have cultivated the higher mathematics for their own sake only, or any further than as they could be applied to the study of the phenomena of nature, or to the practice of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of art: in fact, without some such limitation, there would be no track to guide us in the pathless regions of quantity and number, and their endless relations and functions. But besides the utility of the pure mathematics as a branch of early education, in exercising and fortifying the powers of the mind, it is impossible to foresee with certainty how much of mathematics may be wanted by the natural philosopher in any given <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>; and Professor Robison, as well as many others of his countrymen, would certainly have been the better for the possession of a little more, as the author of the criticisms in the Imperial Review has already had occasion to remark. Philosophical Magazine, xiii.; Dr Gleig, in Antijacobin Magazine, xi. 1802; Stark's Biographia Scotica; Aikin's General Biography, viii. Lond. 1813, 4to; Playfair, in Edinb. Trans. vii. 1815, p. 495; Chalmers's Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, xxv. Lond. 1816, 8vo.

ROBORANTS

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines which strengthen the parts, and give new vigour to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>.

ROCAH

Pages 317-317

a small seaport of Hadramaut, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Ocean, thirty miles south-south-west of Sahar.

ROCHDALE

Pages 317-317

a market-town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, in the hundred of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALFORD">Salford</a>, 197 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and twelve from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>. It is situated in a fine valley on the river Roche, and is overlooked by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which stands on an eminence ascended by 118 steps. The hills around it abound in excellent coal. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> occupation is the manufacture of flannels and other woollen goods. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and contains twelve townships, two of which are in the west riding of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the ten in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> amounted in 1801 to 29,954, in 1811 to 45,227, in 1821 to 48,112, and in 1831 to 58,441; that of the Yorkshire <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> amounted in 1831 to 15,997. By the parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BILL">bill</a> this town has received the privilege of electing one member to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons, but it has no municipal corporation.

ROCHE-BERNARD

Pages 317-317

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORBIHAN">Morbihan</a>, and arrondissement of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VANNES">Vannes</a>. It is situated on the river Vilaine, and contains 1380 inhabitants; but within the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> are 6570 persons, who are chiefly employed in making flaxen thread and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> goods.

ROCHE-CHOUART

Pages 317-317

an arrondissement of the department of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, in France. It extends over 286 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehends five cantons, divided into twenty-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> communes, and contains 48,818 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the town of the same name, on the banks of the river Grenne. It contains 4123 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0.45. E. Lat. 45. 43. N.

ROCHEFORT

Pages 317-317

an arrondissement of the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, in France, which extends over 257 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It comprises four cantons, divided into forty-two communes, and in 1836 contained 51,727 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, about six miles from the mouth of the river Charente. The harbour is convenient and secure, and constantly contains many men of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The wharfs are very well contrived, and vessels can take in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> discharge the guns and other stores with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> facility. It was first made a naval arsenal by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. The city is surrounded with walls, and the harbour defended by strong forts. It is a regular, well-built city, with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets containing five churches, a naval <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, a school of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and fine docks. There were, in 1836, 15,441 inhabitants, besides a garrison in the handsome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. There are establishments for making <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">china</a>, for refining <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and manufactories of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, and sailcloth. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 2. 54. Rochefoucault. W. Lat. 45. 16. 10. N.

ROCHEFOUCAULT

Pages 317-317

Francis <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> de la, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Marillac, governor of Poitou, was born in 1663. He was the son of Francis, the first duke of Rochefoucault, and was distinguished equally by his courage and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. These shining qualities endeared him to all the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, who were ambitious of decorating themselves at once with the laurels of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. He wrote two excellent works; the one a book of Maxims, which, Voltaire says, has contributed more than any thing else to form the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and the other, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Regency of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It was partly at the instigation of the beautiful duchess de Longueville, to whom he had <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been attached, that the duke de Rochefoucault engaged in the civil wars, in which he signalized himself, particularly at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANTOINE">Antoine</a>. After the civil wars were ended, he thought of nothing but enjoying the calm pleasures of friendship and literature. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> became the rendezvous of every person of genius in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>. Racine, Boileau, and Savigné, found in his conversation charms which they sought for in vain elsewhere. He was not, however, with all his elegance and genius, a member of the French Academy. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of making a public speech on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his reception was the only cause that he did not claim admittance. This nobleman, with all the courage he had displayed upon various critical occasions, and with his superiority of birth and understanding over the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> run of men, did not think himself capable of facing an audience to utter only four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in public, without being out of countenance. He died at Paris in 1680, aged sixty-eight, leaving behind him a character which has been variously drawn by those who during his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were proud of his friendship.

ROCHELLE

Pages 317-317

an arrondissement of the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, in France, extending over 282 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It comprehends <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> cantons, divided into fifty-five communes, and in 1836 contained 78,797 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, the seat of the departmental <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and of the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. It is on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, is strongly fortified, and has a convenient and secure harbour defended by two forts. It is the seat of a bishop, has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, one Protestant and five Catholic churches, and in the year 1836 had 14,857 inhabitants, who are traders in wine, brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> products, and in all kinds of colonial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. It is celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> siege when held by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in 1628, which was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for thirteen months, and was attended with dreadful sufferings. Long. 1. 14. 17. W. Lat. 46. 9. 33. N.

ROCHESTER

Pages 317-318

an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, thirty miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to have been founded by the ancient Britons. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it was one of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stations, but did not attain any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celebrity until more than a century after the arrival of the Saxons, who in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a>, constituted it the seat of a bishop, and it was considered as a most important military station. By the Britons it was known under the name of Dourbrus; the Romans called it Durobrivae, which the Saxons changed to Rochester, from which its present name has been derived. It is situated on the river Medway, a stream which, rising in the centre of Kent, becomes navigable at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAIDSTONE">Maidstone</a>, and increases, till near Rochester, it is affected by the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, which reach it from the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at the Nore. At Rochester is the first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over that fine stream. This bridge, built in the reign of King John, with the exception of the bridges in London, was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> deemed superior to any other in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in height, strength, and elegance. It consists of eleven <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, three of which have been rebuilt, and the whole, by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> improvement, widened and beautified, and ornamented with balustrades, panels, and bold copings. The largest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> is forty feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>, and the others thirty feet. The length is 560 feet, and the breadth twenty-four feet between the parapets. The river Medway is capable of receiving the largest vessels up to Rochester, but few are moored off the city, as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the river, is more convenient from the vicinity to the naval arsenal and the docks. The ancient castle is an interesting object to all antiquaries. It stands on the south-west side of the city, on such an elevated spot that it can be seen at thirty miles distance. The streets of this city have no peculiar feature, except the narrowness and length; for in fact it consists chiefly of a single street, which is a continuation of Stroud towards the west and of Chatham towards the east, forming two rows of moderate houses, more than two miles from one end to the other, with a few short streets <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> lanes leading from them southward. With the exception of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, hereafter to be noticed, the town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is the most remarkable edifice: it was built in 1687. It is a handsome structure, with a spacious entrance-hall and staircase, the ceilings of both which are very curiously ornamented. Here the city business is transacted; and at the back <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is the city jail. There is a free school, several charitable institutions, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and a market-house. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Rochester is the smallest in the kingdom. It had a cathedral as early as the year 600, which was destroyed by Ethelbert, king of Mercia, in 676; and a few years after the city suffered much by the incursions of the Danes, but appears to have recovered some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of respectability by the accession of King Athelstan, who appointed masters of the mint to superintend the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The cathedral had been dilapidated at the Norman conquest; but Gundulph, who was removed from Normandy to fill the see, acquired money sufficient to rebuild the sacred edifice, though he died in 1094, before it was finished. Like most of the more ancient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> erections, its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> is an improvement on the basilica of Rome, and it is built in the form of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of Christ, with a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> tower at the point of intersection. The interior space to the west of the cross was the nave or body of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which represented the ship of St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>: this part is more ancient than the nave of any other cathedral in the kingdom, and still retains most of the peculiar features of the style in which it was originally built, and is indeed one of the most interesting specimens of Norman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The whole length of this nave is a hundred and fifty feet, and its breadth between the pillars thirty-three feet, and from one wall to the other seventy-five feet. The choir has an ascent of ten steps, and is a hundred and fifty-six feet in length. The western <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the cathedral, one of the most perfect specimens of Anglo-Norman architecture, was constructed with consummate ability at a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when the art had arrived at a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> point of perfection. The centre door is formed of a semicircular arch, composed of rich <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a>, and is supported by four pillars, with capitals of wreathed foliage. Two of these pillars take the form of Caryatides, and present <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of King Henry I., and his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Matilda, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Malcolm III., king of Scotland, being undoubtedly two of the most ancient statues remaining in England. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> presents many other objects of very high <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to the student and the admirer of ancient architecture. The cathedral contains but few monuments, and none with any striking peculiarity. Rochester is not a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of much trade, except what arises from the great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of travellers passing through it in their way by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> to and from the continent. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> occupation is a considerable oyster-fishery, from beds in the river Medway, which river is under the concurrent jurisdiction of its own corporate body, and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-mayor and aldermen of London. The latter body make periodical visits of conservancy by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and on such occasions the two corporations indulge together in sumptuous festivity. For municipal purposes, the city is divided into three wards, and is governed by a mayor, six aldermen, and seventeen councillors. The recorder and justices of the peace are appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. The city returns two members to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. There is a well-supplied market on Fridays, and several annual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1821 to 8795, and in 1831 to 9811.

ROCHFORD

Pages 318-318

a market-town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, in the hundred of the same name, thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated on a small river that empties itself into the Crouch. It has a good market on Thursday. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1801 to 1228, in 1811 to 1214, in 1821 to 1382, and in 1831 to 1256.

ROCKET

Pages 318-318

an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fire-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, consisting of a cylindrical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, filled with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of certain combustible ingredients; which, being tied to a stick, mounts into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and then bursts. See <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PYROTECHNY">Pyrotechny</a>.

ROCKY MOUNTAINS

Pages 318-320

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mountain chain which traverses the western <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, extending from about latitude 70° north to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, where it is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by the Cordilleras of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>. These ranges are considered as forming part of one vast chain, which in South America, near the equator, attains its greatest elevation. At the Isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> it is so low as nearly to disappear; but this is in conformity with the narrowness of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, and but for a short space. This slight interruption is not sufficient to entitle us to consider the continuity as broken, so that we have in the western hemisphere one great mountain range extending along both continents, from the Polar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> on the north, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORN">Horn</a> on the south, a distance of more than one hundred and twenty degrees of latitude, without including the windings. The eastern side of North America is traversed by a similar range of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called the Alleghanies, which stretch along in continued and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, breadth, and height of the Rocky Mountains are much greater than those of the former. It is however supposed that the Rocky Mountains extend along the western part of the continent, at about the same distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a> that the Alleghanies on the eastern side extend from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>. Although but partially explored, the primitive character of the Rocky Mountains is clearly established. Their eastern sides are covered to the height of two hundred <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> three hundred feet, with a sandstone consisting of the ruins of the granitic rocks upon which it reposes, where disintegration was apparently effected by the gradual agency of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ocean, once occupying the immense plain or basin now extending eastward from the base of these mountains to the chain of the Alleghanies. They have not however been sufficiently explored to admit our advancing any scientific details in regard to them. Many of the detached mountains and prominent peaks have not yet been either named, classified, or described. It does not appear that many of them rise above the region of perpetual refrigeration. But we have the concurrent testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> and Clarke, as well as others, that in latitude 47° north, immense quantities of snow are on their summits, between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSOURI">Missouri</a> and Columbia, in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. They are seen like a vast rampart rising from the grassy plains, stretching from north to south. Sometimes their aspect is that of continued ranges of a grayish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, rising into the blue of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, above the region of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. A great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, ragged, and precipitous; and their bases are strewn with immense boulders and fragments of rock, detached by earthquakes and the elements. From this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-bound and precipitous character they probably received the appellation of Rocky Mountains. Some of the peaks are supposed to be twelve or thirteen thousand feet in height; and the general range is considerably higher than any other in North America, with the exception of the Rodney, George Brydges, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Rodney, was born Rodney, on the 19th of February 1718. He was the descendant of an ancient family, and was related to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Chandos. His father Henry Rodney obtained, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fourteen, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as cornet of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; but having quitted the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> after a short <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he settled at Walton-upon-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and married <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and co-heiress of Sir Henry Newton, envoy extraordinary to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and afterwards judge of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. Through the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the duke, who usually attended the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> on his journeys to and from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, Mr Rodney obtained the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-YACHT">yacht</a>; and having on one of these occasions been asked what mark of favour he would wish the king to confer upon him, he requested that his majesty would stand sponsor for his son. Such a request was easily granted; and accordingly his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son was named after his royal and noble godfathers. At a very early age he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARROW">Harrow</a> school; and having quitted it at the age of twelve, he received from the king a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of service, the last ever granted, and went to sea. On the Newfoundland station he served for six years with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Medley. On the 15th of February 1739 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> in the Dolphin, by Admiral Haddock, in the Mediterranean, and served successively in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, Royal Sovereign, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>. Admiral Mathews having in 1742 appointed him to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> of sixty-four guns, he convoyed three hundred sail of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> trade through the midst of the French fleet, then cruising in the channel; and for his conduct on this occasion he received the warmest thanks of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> he was confirmed by the admiralty, and was appointed to the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a>, in which he continued for eighteen months. He was then removed to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUDLOW">Ludlow</a> Castle, of forty guns. In this ship he fought and took the great St Malo privateer, of forty guns, and one hundred men above his own complement. From this period till <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1745, he was employed in various pieces of service, which afforded him no particular opportunities of obtaining distinction. Having been appointed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CENTURION">Centurion</a>, he for two years cruised in the North Sea; and on that station he commanded while the pretender was in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and until the arrival of Admiral Byng. He was now promoted to the command of the Eagle, of sixty-four guns; and in 1747 he was despatched in a small squadron for the purpose of intercepting the French fleet, homeward-bound from St Domingo. On the 20th of June they fell in with this fleet off Cape Ortegal. The French men-of-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> deserted their convoy during the night, and no fewer than forty-eight merchantmen were captured. Rodney afterwards joined the squadron of Admiral Hawke, and bore a distinguished part in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> off <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a> on the 14th of October in the same year. Near the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of this war, a small squadron, of which the Eagle was one, fell in with a Spanish fleet from the West Indies, consisting of twelve sail of the line with a rich convoy, and, notwithstanding their own inferiority, they took from them six sail of merchantmen. Captain Rodney was appointed to the Rainbow in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1748, and was soon afterwards sent as governor and commander-in-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> on the Newfoundland station. This was his first appearance with the rank of commodore. He had received particular instructions to discover, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Western Ocean, said to be in lat. 49° N., about three hundred leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. After cruising fourteen days to no purpose, he sailed for St John's, the seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In this station he continued till the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October 1752, when he returned home to take his seat in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, having been elected for the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALTASH">Saltash</a>. In May 1757 he sailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, of seventy-four guns, with Hawke's expedition for the bombardment of Rodney; and in February 1758, with Boscawen in the expedition against Louisbourg. On the 19th of May 1759 he was promoted to the rank of rear-admiral, and was immediately appointed to the command of a small squadron destined to bombard <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAVRE">Havre</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>. This service he performed in a very effectual manner; and having continued to keep the sea till the close of the ensuing year, he returned to Britain. In 1761 he was elected member of parliament for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PENRYN">Penryn</a>. On the 6th of October he hoisted his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> on board the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, having been appointed commander-in-chief at Barbadoes and the Leeward <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, and to conduct the naval operations of the armament destined for the attack of Martinique. This island, together with St Lucia, was speedily reduced. The admiral returned home on the 12th of August 1763. On the 21st of the preceding October he had been made vice-admiral of the fleet. In 1764 he was created a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a>, and during the following year was appointed governor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>. In 1768 he was returned to parliament for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>. On the 18th of October 1770 he became vice-admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and on the 24th of October 1771 vice-admiral of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>. During the latter year, on the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, he had been appointed commander-in-chief at Jamaica, and with this command was not permitted to retain the office of governor. Having returned to Britain, he struck his flag at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> on the 4th of September 1774. Being inattentive, as many seamen are, to the rules of economy, his circumstances became so embarrassed that he was obliged to fly from his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with very slight hopes of ever being able to return. He was in France when the ill-advised policy of that court prompted them to take a decided part with America against Great Britain; and it is said that some men in power, no strangers to the desperate state of Sir George's affairs, offered him a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> command in the French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, if he would carry arms against his own country. This offer he rejected with becoming indignation. Soon after this gallant behaviour, the duke de Chartres, afterwards the infamous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, told Sir George that he was himself to have a command in the fleet to be opposed to that under the command of his countryman Keppele; and with an insulting <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> asked him what he thought would be the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their meeting. "That my countryman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry your highness with him to learn English," was the high-spirited reply. These statements do not perhaps rest on sufficient authority; but we learn from his own correspondence, that Maréchal Biron expressed his willingness to advance whatever sum he might require, even to the amount of two thousand pounds. Having accepted a loan of a thousand <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">louis</a>, he was in 1778 enabled to pay his bills in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and to revisit his own country. He was speedily enabled to discharge this debt, and to make a satisfactory arrangement with his creditors. On the 1st of October 1779, Rodney was appointed commander-in-chief of Barbadoes and the Leeward Islands. His first exploit after this appointment was on the 8th of January ensuing, when he took sixteen Spanish transports, together with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ships and vessels of war, which had left St Sebastian's a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> before. On the 16th of the same month he fell in with the Spanish fleet, consisting of eleven sail of the line, under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Juan de Langara; of which one was blown up during the engagement, five were taken and carried into Gibraltar, among which was the admiral's ship, and the rest were much shattered. In April the same year, he fell in with the French fleet under the command of Admiral Guichen, at Martinique, whom he compelled to fight, and whom he completely <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>; though, from the shattered state of his own fleet, and the unwillingness of the enemy to risk another action, he took none of their ships. The successful efforts of the gallant admiral during the year 1780 were generally applauded through the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. He received the thanks of both houses of parliament, and addresses of thanks from various parts of Great Britain, and the islands to which his victories were more particularly serviceable. In December the same year, he made an unsuccessful attempt, together with General Vaughan, on St Vincent's. In 1781, he continued his exertions, with much success, in defending the West <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> Islands; and, along with the above-named general, he conquered St Eustatius, on which occasion his conduct to the inhabitants has been much, though perhaps unjustly, censured. The island was certainly a nest of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a> traders. On the 12th of April 1782, he came to a close action with the French fleet under <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Grasse; during which he sunk one ship and took five, of which the admiral's ship, the Ville de Paris, was one. On the 22nd of May, the thanks of both houses of parliament were voted to the admiral, his officers, and seamen, for this brilliant and decisive victory. He was appointed vice-admiral of Great Britain, and was raised to the peerage by the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Rodney of Stoke in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons voted him an annual pension of £2,000. In the year 1793 this pension was permanently settled on the title; and in 1806 a pension of £1,000 Irish was granted to his grandson for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Having been superseded, very ungraciously, in his command, Lord Rodney once more steered a homeward course. He landed at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> on the 15th of September 1782, and next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> proceeded to join his family at Purbrook near Portsmouth. He survived for ten years, having died on the 24th of May 1792, after he had completed the seventy-fourth year of his age. Lord Rodney had been twice married; first to the sister of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Northampton, and next to the daughter of John Clies, Esq. With her he did not reside for several years before his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was succeeded in his title and estates by his son George, who married, in 1781, Martha, daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Hon. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALDERMAN">Alderman</a> Harley, by whom he had issue.

RODOSTO

Pages 320-320

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALIPOLI">Galipoli</a>. It is situated on a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of the same name, on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> of Marmora. It is strongly fortified, and well built, having, for a Turkish town, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets. It is the seat of a Greek archbishop, has five Greek and two Armenian churches, many mosques, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and caravanserais.
