Numerous sceptics have arisen also in modern times, varying in their principles, manners, and character, as chance, prejudice, vanity, weakness, or indolence, prompted them. The great object, however, which they seem to have in view is to overturn, or at least to weaken, the evidence of analogy, experience, and testimony; though some of them have even attempted to show, that the axioms of geometry are uncertain, and its demonstrations inconclusive. This last attempt has not indeed been often made; but the chief aim of Mr Hume's philosophical writings is to introduce doubts into every branch of physics, metaphysics, history, ethics, and theology. It is needless to give a specimen of his reasonings in support of modern scepticism. The most important of them have been noticed in the articles Miracle, Metaphysics, and Philosophy; and such of our readers as have any relish for speculations of that nature can be no strangers to his Essays, or to the able confutations of them by Reid, Campbell, Gregory, Beattie, and Stewart, who have likewise exposed the weakness of the sceptical reasonings of Descartes, Malebranche, and other philosophers of great fame in the same school. SCEPTRE, a kind of royal staff, borne on solemn occasions by kings, as a badge of their command and authority. Nicod derives the word from the Greek σκῆπτρον, which, he says, originally signified a javelin, which the ancient kings usually bore as a badge of their authority, that instrument being in very great veneration among the heathens. But σκῆπτρον does not properly signify a javelin; it means a staff to rest upon, from σκῆπτος, τιμωρ, I lean upon. Accordingly, in the simplicity of the earlier ages of the world, the sceptres of kings were no other than long walking staves; and Ovid, in speaking of Jupiter, describes him as resting on his sceptre. The sceptre is an ensign of royalty of greater antiquity than the crown. The Greek tragic and other poets put sceptres in the hands of the most ancient kings they introduce. Justin observes, that the sceptre, in its original, was a hasta, or spear. He adds, that, in the most remote antiquity, men adored the haster or sceptres as immortal gods; and that it was upon this account that, even in his time, they still furnished the gods with sceptres. Neptune's sceptre is his trident. Tarquin the Elder was the first who assumed the sceptre among the Romans. Legendre tells us, that, in the first race of the French kings, the sceptre was a golden rod, almost always of the same height with the king who bore it, and crooked at one end like a crozier. Frequently, instead of a sceptre, kings are seen on medals with a palm in their hand. SCHAFFHAUSEN, one of the cantons of Switzerland. It is bounded on the north, east, and west, by the grand duchy of Baden; and on the south by the Rhine, which divides it from the cantons of Thurgau and Zurich. It is only 120 square miles in extent, in which are comprehended three cities, four market-towns, and thirty-five villages. It contains 28,050 inhabitants, who, except about 260 Roman Catholics, adhere to the reformed church. The force to be contributed to the general confederation is fixed at 466 men, and the payment in money at 9320 francs. The chief article

The sceptre is an ensign of royalty of greater antiquity than the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. SCHAFFHAUSEN

Pages 691-692

one of the cantons of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, east, and west, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>; and on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, which divides it from the cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THURGAU">Thurgau</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>. It is only 120 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, in which are comprehended three cities, four market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and thirty-five villages. It contains 28,050 inhabitants, who, except about 260 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, adhere to the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The force to be contributed to the general confederation is fixed at 466 men, and the payment in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a> at 9320 francs. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> article <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCHAMACHI">Schamachi</a> of cultivation is wine, which, though not of the best <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, finds a ready <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SALE">sale</a> in the other cantons, and hence the hills are mostly covered with vineyards. Corn is raised about equal in amount to the consumption, and the meadows feed many cows, which produce much good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. The river Rhine receives all the streams of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANTON">canton</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, about one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> cascade of the Rhine. It is an antique-looking town, with a narrow street and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> houses; it is also walled, and has a citadel. There are three churches, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>; and it contains 7000 inhabitants, who carry on cotton-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>, calico-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, and make caps, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and hosiery. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 32' E. Lat. 47° 42' N.

SCHAMACHI

Pages 692-692

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Shirvan, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, once <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and commercial, but now ruined, and its remains entirely covered with thick brushwood. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is called New Schamachi, and is situated in a plain on the river Akasi, about thirty miles from the Kur, and nearly the same distance from the Caspian. It is built in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, each side of which is eight hundred paces <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and the walls are in tolerable repair, built of unburned brick, and surrounded with a very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and deep ditch. It is supposed to have contained 6000 inhabitants previous to its capture during the late <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> by Aga Mahomed. It was desolated by this <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, and has not recovered from its fallen state. Long. 48° 45' E. Lat. 40° 27' N.

SCHANCK

Cape, a rocky point, with three rocky islets lying off it, on the south coast of New s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland. It is the west point of the principal entrance into Western Port. Long. 144° 53' E. Lat. 38° 30' S.

SCHANTARSKIIJA

three s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands off the eastern coast of Asiatic Russia, in the Sea of Okhotzki. Long. 188° to 139° E. Lat. 55° 15' to 53° 30' N.

SCHAREDSJE

Pages 692-692
or Zaka, an island in the Persian Gulf, near the coast of Arabia, about thirty miles in circumference. Long. 54° 15' E. Lat. 25° N.

SCHASBURG

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Sievenburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of its own name. It contains four Lutheran churches, with a Catholic and a Greek one, 1230 houses, and 7100 inhabitants, chiefly of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>. There is a Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and considerable manufacturing industry employed in making cotton and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> goods. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 43' E. Lat. 46° 10' 9' N.

SCHAUENBURG

Pages 692-692

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the principality of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel, in Germany, adjoining to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIPPE_DETMOLD"><a class="xre</a>f" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-LIPPE">Lippe</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETMOLD">Detmold</a>, and Lippe-Schaumburg. It is 193 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> district, except on such parts as are near the river Weser, which are of moderate fertility. It comprehends five <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and 130 villages and hamlets, with 28,600 inhabitants, whose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> occupation, besides that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. It produces some good coal, and abundance of wood. It is divided into three bailiwicks, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rentelen, on the Weser, containing 2850 inhabitants.

SCHAUENBURG-LIPPE

Pages 692-692

a small independent principality in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Germany, between <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> on the north and north-east, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel on the east and south-east, and the Prussian Westphalian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> on the south-west and the west. It extends over 210 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and comprehends two small cities, three market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 108 villages, with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 23,128 persons, who all adhere to the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, except 3600 Calvinists and about 100 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. The revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> amount to about L.21,500, wholly drawn from his domains, no taxes of any kind being demanded; and as the reigning prince was in his minority during the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the greatest suffering in this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Germany, his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> managed so prudently as to leave him without any debt. The principality is bound to provide a force of 240 men to the German confederation. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is undulating, but there are no hills of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, and all are capable of cultivation. It rises gradually from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Weser, into which run all the streams of the principality. It has one <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, the Steinbader, nearly fifty miles in compass, on which is a strong fortress used as an arsenal, and it is most abundantly stocked with fish. It has some valuable mineral <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; one near Stadthagen is resorted to for curative purposes. There are some valuable coal-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> worked, which belong to the prince, and are said to form one <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of his revenue. There are many flocks of sheep, some yielding fine <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> from the native races having been crossed by merinos. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produces more corn than is consumed; and it, with wool, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, wood, and coal, are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> objects of trade. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is Buckeberg, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of 4220 inhabitants, on a gradual ascent from the Weser, and six miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINDEN">Minden</a>.

SCHAZK

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, within the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TAMBOV">Tambov</a>. It is 737 miles from St Petersburg, on the river Schazk. It is old and ill built, and contains eight churches, only three of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, 1101 houses, with 6800 inhabitants, chiefly making hempen goods, and cultivating that plant. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 41° 49' E. Lat. 54° 26' N.

SCHECHE SURE

or SURDE, a small island in the Persian Gulf, with a village on the southern coast, where water and provisions may be obtained. Long. 54° 30' E. Lat. 26° 8' N.

SCHEDUAN

an immense naked rock in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> and five <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, at nearly an equal distance from the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. SCHEDULE

a scroll of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, annexed to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>, lease, or other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, containing an inventory of goods, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> omitted in the body of the deed. The word is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of the Latin scheda, or Greek σχέδιον, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> or piece of paper.

SCHEELE

Pages 692-693
CHARLES WILLIAM, was born on the 19th of December 1742, at Stralsund, where his father had kept a shop. When he was very young, he received the usual instructions of a private school; and was afterwards advanced to an academy. At a very early age he showed a strong desire to follow the profession of an apothecary, and his father suffered him to gratify his inclinations. With Mr Bauch, an apothecary at Gottenburg, he served his apprenticeship, which was completed in six years. He remained, however, some time longer at that place, and it was there that he so excellently laid the foundations of his knowledge. Among the various books which he read that treated of chemical subjects, Kuncell's Laboratory seems to have been his favourite. He used to repeat many of the experiments contained in that work privately in the night, when the rest of the family had retired to rest. A friend of Scheele's had remarked the progress which he had made in chemistry, and had asked him by what inducements he had at first been led to study a science in which he had gained such knowledge. Scheele replied, "The first cause, my friend, arose from yourself. Nearly at the beginning of my apprenticeship you advised me to read Neuman's Chemistry, from the perusal of which I became eager to make experiments myself; and I remember very well how I mixed together, in a conserve-glass, oil of cloves and fuming acid of nitre, which immediately took fire. I see also still before my eyes an unlucky experiment which I made with pyrophorus. Circumstances of this kind did but the more inflame my desire to repeat experiments." After Scheele's departure from Gottenburg in the year 1765, he obtained a place with Kalstrom, an apothecary at Malmo. Two years afterwards he went from thence to Stockholm, and managed the shop of Mr Scharenberg. In 1773, he changed this appointment for another at Upsal, under Mr Loock. Here he was fortunately situated, as, from his acquaintance with learned men, and from having free access to the university laboratory, he had opportunities of increasing his knowledge. At this place also he happily commenced the friendship which subsisted between him and Bergman. During his residence at this place, Prince Henry of Prussia, accompanied by the Duke of Sodermania, visited Upsal, and chose this opportunity to see the academical laboratory. Scheele was accordingly appointed by the university to exhibit to them some chemical experiments. This office he undertook, and showed some of the most curious processes in chemistry. The two princes asked him many questions, and expressed their approbation of the answers which he returned to them. The duke asked him of what country he was, and seemed to be much pleased when Scheele informed him that he was born at Stralsund. At their departure they told the professor, who was present, that they should esteem it a favour if he would permit the young man to have free access to the laboratory as often as he chose to make experiments. In the year 1777 Scheele was appointed by the Medical College to be apothecary at Koping. It was at that place that he soon showed the world how great a man he was, and that no place or situation could confine his abilities. When he was at Stockholm he showed his acuteness as a chemist, as he discovered there the new and wonderful acid contained in the fluor spar. It has been confidently asserted that Scheele was the first who discovered the nature of the aerial acid, and that whilst he was at Upsal he made many experiments to prove its properties. This circumstance might probably have furnished Bergman with the means of treating this subject more fully. At the same place he began the series of excellent experiments on that remarkable mineral substance manganese; from which investigation he was led to make the very valuable and interesting discovery of oxymuriatic acid. At the same time he examined the properties of ponderous earth. At Koping he finished his Dissertation on Air and Fire; a work which the celebrated Bergman most warmly recommended in the friendly preface which he wrote for it. The theory which Scheele endeavours to prove in this treatise is, that fire consists of pure air and phlogiston. According to more recent opinions, if inflammable air be phlogiston, water is composed of these two principles. Of these opinions we may say, in the words of Cicero, "Opiniones tam variae sunt: tamque inter se dissidentes ut alterum profecto fieri potest ut earum nulla, alterum certe non potest ut plus una vera sit." The author's merit in this work, exclusive of the encomiums of Bergman, was sufficient to obtain the approbation of the public; as the ingenuity displayed in treating so delicate a subject, and the many new and valuable observations which are dispersed through the treatise, justly entitled the author to that fame which his book procured him. It was spread abroad throughout every country, became soon out of print, and was reprinted, and translated into many languages. The English translation is enriched with the notes of that accurate and truly philosophical genius Mr Richard Kirwan. Scheele now diligently employed himself in contributing to the Transactions of the Academy at Stockholm. He first pointed out a new way to prepare the salt of benzoin. In the same year he discovered that arsenic, freed in a particular manner from phlogiston, partakes of all the properties of an acid, and has its peculiar affinities to other substances. In a Dissertation on Flint, Clay, and Alum, he clearly overturned Beaumé's opinion of the identity of the siliceous and argillaceous earths. He published an Analysis of the Human Calculus. He showed also a mode of preparing mercurius dulcis in the humid way, and improved the process of making the powder of algaroth. He analysed the mineral substance called molybdena, or flexible black lead. Scheele discovered a beautiful green pigment. He showed us how to decompose the air of the atmosphere. He discovered that some neutral salts are decomposed by lime and by iron. He decomposed plumbago, or the common black lead. He observed, with peculiar ingenuity, an acid in milk, which decomposes acetated alkali; and in his experiments on the sugar of milk, he discovered another acid, different in some respects from the above-mentioned acids and the common acid of sugar. He accomplished the decomposition of tungsten, the component parts of which were before unknown, and found in it a peculiar metallic acid united to lime. He published an excellent dissertation on the different sorts of ether. He found out an easy way to preserve vinegar for many years. His investigation of the colouring matter in Prussian blue, the means he employed to separate it, and his discovery that alkali, sal ammoniac, and charcoal, mixed together, will produce it, are strong marks of his penetration and genius. He found out a peculiar sweet matter in expressed oils after they have been boiled with litharge and water. He showed how the acid of lemons may be obtained in crystals. He found the white powder in rhubarb, which Model thought to be selenite, and which amounts to one seventh of the weight of the root, to be calcareous earth united to the acid of sorrel. This suggested to him the examination of the acid of sorrel. He precipitated acetate of lead with it, and decomposed the precipitate thus obtained by the vitriolic acid, and by this process he obtained the common acid of sugar; and by slowly dropping a solution of fixed alkali into a solution of the acid of sugar, he regenerated the acid of sorrel. From his examination of the acids contained in fruits and berries, he found not one species of acid alone, viz. the acid of lemon, but also another, which he denominated the malaceous or malic acid, from its being found in the greatest quantity in apples. By the decomposition of Bergman's new metal, siderite, he showed the truth of Meyer's and Klavroth's conjecture concerning it. He boiled the calx of siderite with alkali of tartar, and precipitated nitrate of mercury by the middle salt which he obtained by this operation. The calx of mercury which was precipitated was found to be united to the acid of phosphorus, so that he demonstrates that this calx was phosphoretted iron. He found also that the native Prussian blue contained the same acid. He discovered, by the same means, that the perlute acid, as it was called, was not an acid sui generis, but the phosphoric united to a small quantity of the mineral alkali. He suggested an improvement in the process for obtaining magnesia from Epsom salt; and he advises the adding of an equal weight of common salt to the Epsom salt, so that an equal weight of Glauber's salt may be obtained; but this will not succeed unless during the cold of winter. These are the valuable discoveries of this great philosopher, which are to be found in the Transactions of the Royal Society at Stockholm. Most of his essays have been published in French by Madame Picardet and M. Morveau of Dijon. Dr Beddoes also has made a very valuable present to his countrymen of an English translation of a great part of Scheele's dissertations, to which he has added some useful and ingenious notes. Viewing Scheele as a philosopher, we must judge of him from his many and important discoveries. What concerns him as a man we are informed of by his friends, who affirm that his moral character was irreproachable. It was matter of remark, that his chemical apparatus was neither neat nor convenient; his laboratory was small and confined; nor was he particular in regard to the vessels which he employed in his experiments, so that we may justly wonder how such discoveries and such experiments could have been made. He understood none of the modern languages except the German and Swedish; and he had not the advan-

SCHEINER

Pages 694-694

CHRISTOPHER**, a German mathematician and astronomer, eminent for being the first who discovered spots on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, was born at Schwaben, in the territory of Middleheim, in 1575. He first discovered spots on the sun's disk in 1611, and made observations on these phenomena at Rome, until at length reducing them to order, he published them in one volume folio in 1630. He wrote also some smaller things relating to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and died in 1660.

SCHELDT

Pages 694-694

a river which rises on the confines of Picardy, and runs <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by Cambrai, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VALENCIENNES">Valenciennes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURNAY">Tournay</a>, and Oudenarde, and receiving the Lis at Ghent, runs east by Dendermonde, and then north to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>. Below this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> it divides into two branches, one called the Wester Scheldt, which separates <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> from Zeeland, and discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> near Flushing; and the other called the Ooster-Scheldt, which runs by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol4.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom, and afterwards between the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> Beveland and Schoven, and a little below falls into the sea.

SCHELESTADT

an arrondissement of the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in France, extending over 257,945 acres, equal to 403 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is divided into eight cantons, and these into 114 communes, with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, in 1836, of 134,887 persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated on a canal connected with the river Ill. It is well built and strongly fortified, and contained in the same year 9700 inhabitants, who make <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, hosiery, clocks, wax-lights, and much <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 26'. E. Lat. 48° 17'. N.

a draught <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> representation of any geometrical or astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or problem, by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> sensible to the eye, or of the celestial bodies in their proper places for any moment. It is otherwise called a diagram.

SCHEMNITZ

Pages 694-699

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Hither Danube, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle to which it gives the name. It stands on a lofty situation, 2170 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in a district abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and at the source of the river Scheznitz. It is wildly built, some of the streets being separated from others by rocks, woods, and gardens, especially in the extensive suburbs, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of which equals that within the walls. It contains one Lutheran and four Roman Catholic churches, 1720 houses, with 20,450 inhabitants. It has establishments for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, of both religions; and also a mining academy, with five professors and 150 students. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> seat of the operations of mining; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, arsenic, and sulphur are procured and prepared for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, the value of which is said to exceed L200,000 annually. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18° 48'. 45'. E. Lat. 48° 47'. 45'. N. they did for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> and for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> eclipsed what they had designed for Germany. After them there was a long interlunar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of darkness for the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and the Danube. The German energy, too spasmodically excited, suffered a collapse. Throughout the whole of the seventeenth century, but one vigorous mind arose for permanent effects in literature. This was Opitz, a poet who deserves even yet to be read with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, but who is no more worthy to be classed as the Dryden whom his too partial countrymen have styled him, than the Germany of the Thirty Years' <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">War</a> of taking <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> by the side of civilized and cultured England during the Cromwellian era, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Klopstock of sitting on the same throne with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>. Leibnitz was the one sole potentate in the fields of intellect whom the Germany of this century produced; and he, like <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and Kepler, impresses us rather as a European than as a German mind, partly perhaps from having pursued his self-development in foreign lands, partly from his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> circle of foreign connections, but most of all from his having written chiefly in French or in Latin. Passing onwards to the eighteenth century, we find, through its earlier half, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> wilderness, unclaimed and without <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> vegetation, as the barren arena on which the few insipid writers of Germany paraded. The torpor of academic dulness dominated over the length and breadth of the land. And as these academic bodies were universally found harnessed in the equipage of petty courts, it followed that the lethargies of pedantic dulness were uniformly deepened by the lethargies of aulic and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> dulness; so that, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the reader represents to himself the very <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of birthday odes, sycophantish dedications, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> sermons, he <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> have some adequate idea of the sterility and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> formality which at that era spread the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> over German literature. Literature, the very word literature, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> of scorn to what passed under that name during the period of Gottsched. That such a man indeed as this Gottsched, equal at the best to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of a Latin <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> or a school <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, should for a moment have presided over the German <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, stands out as in itself a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> and significant memorial, too certain for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>, and yet almost too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>; of the apoplectic sleep under which the mind of central <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> at that era lay oppressed. The rust of disuse had corroded the very principles of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. And, as if the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> night of academic dulness, combined with the dulness of court inanities, had not been sufficient for the stifling of all native energies, the feebleness of French models (and of these moreover naturalized through still feebler imitations) had become the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and standard for all attempts at original composition. The darkness of night, it is usually said, grows deeper as it approaches the dawn; and the very enormity of that prostration under which the German intellect at this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> groaned, was the most certain pledge to any observing eye of that intense re-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> soon to stir and kindle among the smouldering activities of this spell-bound people. This re-action, however, was not abrupt and theatrical: it moved through slow stages and by equable gradations: it might be said to commence from the middle of the eighteenth century, that is, about <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years before the birth of Schiller; but a progress of forty years had not carried it so far towards its meridian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>, as that the sympathetic shock from the French Revolution was by one fraction more rude and shattering than the public torpor still demanded. There is a memorable correspondency throughout all members of Protestant Christendom in whatsoever relates to literature and intellectual advance. However imperfect the organization which binds them together, it was sufficient even in these elder times to transmit reciprocally from one to every other, so much of that illumination which could be gathered into books, that no Christian state could be much in advance of another; supposing that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> opposed no barriers to free <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, unless only in those points which depended upon local gifts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, upon the genius of a particular people, or upon the excellence of its institutions. These advantages were incommunicable; let the freedom of intercourse have been what it might: England could not send off by posts or by heralds her iron and coals; she could not send the indomitable energy of her population; she could not send the absolute security of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; she could not send the good <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of her parliaments. These were gifts indigenous to herself, either through the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> of her people, or through the original endowments of her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. But her condition of moral sentiment, her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-toned civic elevation, her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> feeling and popular boldness,—much of these she could and did transmit, by the radiation of the press, to the very extremities of the German empire. Not only were our books translated, but it is notorious to those acquainted with German <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>, or other pictures of German <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, that as early as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Years' War (1756–1763), in fact, from the very era when Cave and Dr Johnson first made the parliamentary debates accessible to the English themselves, most of the German journals repeated, and sent forward as by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a>, these senatorial displays to every village throughout Germany. From the polar latitudes to the Mediterranean, from the mouths of the Rhine to the Euxine, there was no other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of free <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELIBERATIVE">deliberative</a> eloquence in any popular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. And the Luise of Voss alone, a metrical idyll not less valued for its <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of portraiture than our own <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VICAR">Vicar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAKEFIELD">Wakefield</a>, will show, that the most sequestered clergyman of a rural <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> did not think his breakfast equipage complete without the latest report from the great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> that sat in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Hence we need not be astonished that German and English literature were found by the French Revolution in pretty nearly the same condition of semi-vigilance and imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>. That mighty event reached us both, reached us all, we may say (speaking of Protestant states), at the same moment, by the same tremendous <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol9.html#article-GALVANISM">galvanism</a>. The snake, the intellectual snake, that lay in ambush among all nations, roused itself, sloughed itself, renewed its youth, in all of them at the same period. A new world opened upon us all; new revolutions of thought arose; new and nobler activities were born; and other palms were won. But by and through Schiller it was, as its main organ, that this great revolutionary impulse expressed itself. Already, as we have said, not less than forty years before the earthquake by which France exploded and projected the scoria of her huge <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> over all Christian lands, a stirring had commenced among the dry <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of intellectual Germany; and symptoms arose that the breath of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> would soon disturb, by nobler agitations than by petty personal quarrels, the death-like repose even of the German <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. Precisely in those bodies however it was, in those as connected with tyrannical governments, each academic body being shackled to its own petty centre of local despotism, that the old spells remained unlinked; and to them, equally remarkable as firm <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of truth, and as obstinate depositaries of darkness or of superannuated <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, we must ascribe the slowness of the German movement on the path of reascent. Meantime the earliest torch-bearer to the murky literature of this great land, this crystallisation of political states, was Bodmer. This man had no demoniac genius, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> required; but he had some <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and, what was better, he had some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. He lived among the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a> lay among the alpine sublimities of Milton and Shakspeare. Through his very eyes he imbibed a daily scorn of Gottsched and his monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of German coarseness with French sensual levity. He could not look at his native Alps, but he <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in them, and their austere <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> or their dread realities, a spiritual reproach to the hollowness and falsehood of that dull imposture which Gottsched offered by way of substitute for nature. He was taught by the Alps to crave for something nobler and deeper. Bodmer, though far below such a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, rose by favour of circumstances into an <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> or missionary of truth for Germany. He translated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of English literature. He inculcated with his own sympathies the more fervent mind of the youthful Klopstock, who visited him in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. And it soon became evident that Germany was not dead, but sleeping; and once again, legibly for any eye, the pulses of life began to play freely through the vast organization of central Europe. Klopstock, however, though a fervid, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, and for that reason an anti-Gallican mind, was himself an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>. Such at least is our own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of this poet. He was the child and creature of enthusiasm, but of enthusiasm not allied with a masculine intellect, or any organ for that capacious vision and meditative range which his subjects demanded. He was essentially thoughtless, betrays everywhere a most effeminate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of sensibility, and is the sport of that pseudo-enthusiasm and baseless rapture which we see so often allied with the excitement of strong liquors. In taste, or the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of proportions and congruences, or the harmonious adaptations, he is perhaps the most defective writer extant. But if no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of German literature, in the sense of having shaped the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> in which it was to flow, in the sense of having disciplined its taste or excited its rivalry by classical models of excellence, or raised a finished standard of style, perhaps we must concede that, on a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, Klopstock did something of that service in every one of these departments. His works were at least Miltonic in their choice of subjects, if ludicrously non-Miltonic in their treatment of those subjects. And, whether due to him or not, it is undeniable that in his time the mother-tongue of Germany revived from the most absolute <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> on record, to its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> purity. In the time of Gottsched, the authors of Germany wrote a macaronic jargon, in which French and Latin made up a considerable proportion of every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: nay, it happened often that foreign words were inflicted with German forms; and the whole result was such as to remind the reader of the medical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> in the *Malade Imaginaire* of Molière, Quid poetae est à faire? Saignaire Balnare Ensuia pargre, &c. Now is it reasonable to ascribe some share in the restoration of good to Klopstock, both because his own writings exhibit nothing of this most abject euphemism (a euphemism expressing itself not in fantastic refinements on the staple of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, but altogether in rejecting it for foreign words and idioms), and because he wrote expressly on the subject of style and composition. Wieland, meantime, if not enjoying so intense an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACCEPTION">acception</a> as Klopstock, had a more extensive one; and it is in vain to deny him the praise of a festive, brilliant, and most versatile <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. The Schlegels showed the haughty malignity of their ungenerous natures, in depreciating Wieland, at a time when old <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> had laid a freezing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> upon the energy which he would once have put forth in defending himself. He was the Voltaire of Germany, and very much more than the Voltaire; for his romantic and legendary poems are above the level of Voltaire. But, on the other hand, he was a Voltaire in sensual <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>. To <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, to carry on a plot, to affect his readers by voluptuous impressions,—these were the unworthy aims of Wieland; and though a good-natured critic would not refuse to make some allowance for a youthful poet's aberrations in this respect, Schiller yet the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> cannot extend itself to mature years. An old man corrupting his readers, attempting to corrupt them, or relying for his effect upon corruptions already effected, in the purity of their affections, is a hideous object; and that must be a precarious influence indeed which depends for its durability upon the licentiousness of men. Wieland, therefore, except in parts, will not last as a national idol; but such he was nevertheless for a time. Bürger wrote too little of any expansive compass to give the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of his powers, or to found national <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LICHTENBERG">Lichtenberg</a>, though a very sagacious observer, never rose into what can be called a power—he did not modify his age; yet these were both men of extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, and Bürger a man of undoubted genius. On the other hand, Lessing was merely a man of talent, but of talent in the highest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> adapted to popularity. His very defects, and the shallowness of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, promoted his popularity; and by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the French critics on the dramatic or scenical proprieties he is ever profound. His plummet, if not suited to the soundless depths of Shakespeare, was able ten times over to fathom the little rivulets of Parisian philosophy. This he did effectually, and thus unconsciously levelled the paths for Shakespeare, and for that supreme dominion which he has since held over the German stage, by crushing with his sarcastic shrewdness the pretensions of all who stood in the way. At that time, and even yet, the functions of a literary man were very important in Germany: the popular mind and the popular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> pointed one way, those of the little courts another. Multitudes of little German states (many of which were absorbed since 1816 by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of *medialization*) made it their ambition to play at keeping mimic armies in their pay, and to ape the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> sovereigns, by encouraging French literature only, and the French language at their courts. It was this latter propensity which had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> the anomalous macaronic dialect, of which we have already spoken as a characteristic circumstance in the social features of literary Germany during the first half of the eighteenth century. Nowhere else, within the records of human follies, do we find a corresponding <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the patrician orders in the state, taking for granted, and absolutely postulating the utter worthlessness for intellectual aims of those in and by whom they maintained their own grandeur and independence, undisguisedly and even professedly sought to ally themselves with a foreign literature, foreign literati, and a foreign language. In this unexampled display of scorn for native resources, and the consequent collision between the two principles of action, all depended upon the people themselves. For a time the wicked and most profligate contempt of the local governments for that native merit which it was their duty to evoke and to cherish, naturally enough produced its own <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>. Like Jews or slaves, whom all the world have agreed to hold contemptible, the German literati found it hard to make head against so obstinate a prejudice; and too often they became all that they were presumed to be. *Sint Macerates, non derunt, Flore, Marones.* And the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> too often holds good—that when all who should have smiled scowl upon a man, he turns out the abject thing they have predicted. Where Frenchified Fredericks sit upon German thrones, it should not surprise us to see a crop of Gottscheds arise as the best fruitage of the land. But when there is any latent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> in the popular mind, such scorn, by its very extremity, will call forth its own counteraction. It was perhaps good for Germany that a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> so eminent in one aspect as *Fritz der einziger,* should put on record so emphatically his intense conviction, that no good thing could arise out of Ger- --- 1 "Freddy the unique;" which is the name by which the Prussians expressed their admiration of their martial and indomitable, though somewhat fantastic, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>. This creed was expressed by the quality of the French minds which he attracted to his court. The very refuse and dregs of the Parisian coteries satisfied his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> for French garbage; the very offal of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHAMBLES">shambles</a> met the demand of his palate; even a Maupertuis, so long as he could produce a French baptismal certificate, was good enough to manufacture into the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> academy. Such scorn challenged a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a>: the contest lay between the thrones of Germany and the popular intellect, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> result was inevitable. Once aware that they were insulted, once enlightened to the full consciousness of the scorn which trampled on them as intellectual and predestined <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HELOTS">Helots</a>, even the mild-tempered Germans became fierce, and now began to aspire, not merely under the ordinary instincts of personal ambition, but with a vindictive feeling, and as conscious agents of retribution. It became a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> with the German author, that the very same works which elevated himself, wreaked his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> upon their princes, and poured retorted scorn upon their most ungenerous and unparental sovereigns. Already, in the reign of the martial Frederick, the men who put most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of authority into his contempt of Germans,—Euler, the matchless Euler, Lambert, and Immanuel Kant,—had vindicated the pre-eminence of German <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. Already, in 1755, had the same Immanuel Kant, whilst yet a probationer for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of logic in a Prussian university, sketched the outline of that philosophy which has secured the admiration, though not the assent, of all men known and proved to have understood it, of all men able to state its doctrines in terms admissible by its disciples. Already, and even previously, had Haller, who wrote in German, placed himself at the head of the current physiology. And in the fields of science or of philosophy, the victory was already decided for the German intellect in competition with the French. But the fields of literature were still comparatively barren. Klopstock was at least an anomaly; Lessing did not present himself in the impassioned walks of literature; Herder was viewed too much in the exclusive and professional <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a clergyman; and, with the exception of John Paul Richter, a man of most original genius, but quite unfitting for general popularity, no commanding mind arose in Germany with powers for levying homage from foreign nations, until the appearance, as a great scencical poet, of Frederick Schiller. The father of this great poet was Caspar Schiller, an officer in the military service of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Würtemberg. He had previously served as a surgeon in the Bavarian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but on his final return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Würtemberg, and to the service of his native prince, he laid aside his medical character for ever, and obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as ensign and adjutant. In 1763, the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> threw him out of his military employment, with the nominal rank of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. But, having conciliated the duke's favour, he was still borne on the books of the ducal establishment; and, as a planner of ornamental gardens, or in some other civil capacity, he <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to serve his serene highness for the rest of his life. The parents of Schiller were both pious, upright persons, with that loyal fidelity to duty, and that humble simplicity of demeanour towards their superiors, which is so often found among the unpretending natives of Germany. It is probable, however, that Schiller owed to his mother exclusively the preternatural endowments of his intellect. She was of humble origin, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a baker, and not so fortunate as to have received much education. But she was apparently rich in gifts of the heart and the understanding. She read <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> with delight; and through the profound <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with which she had inspired her son, she found it easy to communicate her own literary tastes. Her husband was not illiterate, and had in mature life so laudably applied himself to the improvement of his own defective knowledge, that at length he thought himself capable of appearing before the public as an author. His book related simply to the subjects of his professional <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> as a horticulturist, and was entitled Die Baumzucht im Grossen (On the Management of Forests). Some merit we must suppose it to have had, since the public called for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of it long after his own death, and even after that of his illustrious son. And although he was a plain man, of no pretensions, and possibly even of slow faculties, he has left behind him a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, in which there is one petition of sublime and pathetic piety, worthy to be remembered by the side of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AGUR">Agur</a>'s wise prayer against the almost equal temptations of poverty and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. At the birth of his son, he had been reflecting with sorrowful anxiety, not unmingled with self-reproach, on his own many disqualifications for conducting the education of the child. But at length, reading in his own manifold imperfections but so many reiterations of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> that he should rely upon God's bounty, converting his very defects into so many arguments of hope and confidence in heaven, he prayed thus: "Oh God, that knowest my poverty in good gifts for my son's inheritance, graciously permits that, even as the want of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> became to thy Son's hunger-stricken flock in the wilderness the pledge of overflowing abundance, so likewise my darkness may, in its sad extremity, carry with it the measure of thy unfathomable light; and because I, thy worm, cannot give to my son the least of blessings, do thou give the greatest; because in my <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> there is not any thing, do thou from thine pour out all things; and that temple of a new-born spirit, which I cannot adorn even with earthly ornaments of dust and ashes, do thou irradiate with the celestial adornment of thy presence, and finally with that peace that passeth all understanding." Reared at the feet of parents so pious and affectionate, Schiller would doubtless <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a happy childhood; and probably to this utter tranquillity of his earlier years, to his seclusion from all that could create pain, or even anxiety, we must ascribe the unusual dearth of anecdotes from this period of his life; a dearth which has tempted some of his biographers into improving and embellishing some puerile stories, which a man of sense will inevitably reject as too trivial for his gravity or too fantastical for his faith. That nation is happy, according to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> adage, which furnishes little business to the historian; for such a vacuity in facts argues a condition of perfect peace and silent prosperity. That childhood is happy, or may generally be presumed such, which has furnished few records of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> experience, little that has appeared in doing or in suffering to the eyes of companions; for the child who has been made happy by early thoughtfulness, and by infantine struggles with the great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of his origin and his destination (ideas which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> with a deep, dove-like brooding upon the mind of childhood, more than of mature life, vexed with inroads from the noisy world), will not manifest the workings of his spirit by much of external activity. The fallentis semita vitae, that path of noiseless life, which eludes and deceives the conscious notice both of its subject and of all around him, opens equally to the man and to the child; and the happiest of all childhoods will have been that of which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> has survived and expressed itself, not in distinct records, but in deep affection, in abiding love, and the hauntings of meditative power. Such a childhood, in the bosom of maternal tenderness, was probably passed by Schiller; and his first awakening to the world of strife and perplexity happened in his fourteenth year. Up to that period his life had been vagrant, agreeably to the shifting necessities of the ducal service; and his education desultory and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>. But in the year 1773 he was solemnly entered as a member of a new acade- Schiller's medical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, founded by the reigning duke, and recently translated to his little capital of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUTTGART">Stuttgart</a>. This change took <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the special request of the duke, who, under the mask of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, took upon himself the severe control of the whole simple family. The parents were probably both too humble and dutiful in spirit towards one whom they regarded in the double light of sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">lord</a> and of personal benefactor, ever to murmur at the ducal behests, far less to resist them. The duke was for them an earthly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>; and they resigned themselves, together with their child, to the disposal of him who dispensed their earthly blessings, not less meekly than of Him whose viceregent they presumed him to be. In such a frame of mind, requests are but another name for commands; and thus it happened that a second change arose upon the first, even more determinately fatal to the young Schiller's happiness. Hitherto he had cherished a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-dream pointing to the pastoral office in some rural district, as that which would harmonize best with his intellectual purposes, with his love of quiet, and, by means of its preparatory requirements, best also with his own peculiar choice of studies. But this scheme he now found himself compelled to sacrifice; and the two evils which fell upon him concurrently in his new situation were, first, the formal military <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and monotonous routine of duty; secondly, the uncongenial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the studies, which were shaped entirely to the attainment of legal knowledge, and the narrow service of the local tribunals. So illiberal and so exclusive a system of education was revolting to the expansive mind of Schiller; and the military <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> under which this system was enforced, shocked the aspiring nobility of his moral nature, not less than the technical narrowness of the studies shocked his understanding. In point of expense the whole establishment cost nothing at all to those parents who were privileged servants of the duke; in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> were the parents of Schiller, and that single consideration weighed too powerfully upon his filial piety to allow of his openly murmuring at his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>; while on their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> the parents were equally shy of encouraging a disgust which too obviously tended to defeat the promises of ducal favour. This system of monotonous confinement was therefore carried to its completion, and the murmurs of the young Schiller were either dutifully suppressed, or found vent only in secret letters to a friend. In one point only Schiller was able to improve his condition; jointly with the juristic department, was another for training young aspirants to the medical profession. To this, as promising a more enlarged scheme of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, Schiller by permission transferred himself in 1775. But whatever relief he might find in the nature of his new studies, he found none at all in the system of personal discipline which prevailed. Under the oppression of this detested system, and by pure reaction against its wearing persecutions, we learn from Schiller himself, that in his nineteenth year he undertook the earliest of his surviving plays, the Robbers, beyond doubt the most tempestuous, the most volcanic, we might say, of all juvenile creations anywhere recorded. He himself calls it "a monster," and a monster it is; but a monster which has never failed to convulse the heart of young readers with the temperament of intellectual enthusiasm and sensibility. True it is, and nobody was more aware of that fact than Schiller himself in after years, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the three Moors, father and sons, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> impossibilities; and some readers, in whom the judicious acquaintance with human life in its realities has outrun the sensibilities, are so much shocked by these supernatural phenomena, that they are incapable of enjoying the terrific sublimities which on that basis of the visionary do really exist. A poet, perhaps Schiller might have alleged, is entitled to assume hypothetically so much in the previous positions or circumstances of his agents as is requisite to the basis from which he starts. It is undeniable that Shakespeare and others have availed themselves of this principle, and with memorable success. Shakespeare, for instance, postulates his witches, his Caliban, his Ariel: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, he virtually says, such modes of spiritual existence or of spiritual relations as a possibility; do not expect me to demonstrate this, and upon that single concession I will rear a superstructure that shall be self-consistent; every thing shall be internally coherent and reconciled, whatever be its external relations as to our human experience. But this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a>, on the largest scale, is more within the limits of credibility and plausible verisimilitude when applied to modes of existence, which, after all, are in such total darkness to us (the limits of the possible being so undefined and shadowy as to what can or cannot exist), than the very slightest liberties taken with human character, or with those principles of action, motives, and feelings, upon which men would move under given circumstances, or with the modes of action which in common <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> they would be likely to adopt. The truth is, that, as a coherent work of art, the Robbers is indefensible; but, however monstrous it may be pronounced, it possesses a power to agitate and console, which will always obliterate its great faults to the young, and to all whose judgment is not too much developed. And the best apology for Schiller is found in his own words in recording the circumstances and causes under which this anomalous production arose. "To escape," says he, "from the formalities of a discipline which was odious to my heart, I sought a retreat in the world of ideas and shadowy possibilities, while as yet I knew nothing at all of that human world from which I was harshly secluded by iron bars. Of men, the actual men in this world below, I knew absolutely nothing at the time when I composed my Robbers. Four hundred human beings, it is true, were my fellow-prisoners in this abode; but they were mere tautologies and reiterations of the selfsame mechanic creature, and like so many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> casts from the same original statue. Thus situated, of necessity I failed. In making the attempt, my chisel brought out a monster, of which [and that was fortunate] the world had no <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> or resemblance to show." Meantime this demoniac drama produced very opposite results to Schiller's reputation. Among the young men of Germany it was received with an enthusiasm absolutely unparalleled, though it is perfectly untrue that it excited some persons of rank and splendid expectations (as a current <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> asserted) to imitate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Moor in becoming robbers. On the other hand, the play was of too powerful a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> not in any case to have alarmed his serenity the Duke of Würtemberg; for it argued a most revolutionary mind, and the utmost audacity of self-will. But besides this general ground of censure, there arose a special one, in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> so remote that this one fact may serve to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as well as intensity of the impression made. The territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a> had been called by Spiegelberg, one of the robbers, "the Thief's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>." Upon this the magistrates of that country presented a complaint to the duke; and his highness, having cited Schiller to his presence, and severely reprimanded him, issued a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> that this dangerous young student should henceforth confine himself to his medical studies. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> which followed exhibits such extraordinary exertions of despotism, even for that land of irresponsible power, that we must presume the duke to have relied more upon the hold which he had upon Schiller through his affection for parents so absolutely dependent on his highness's power, than upon any laws, good or bad, which he could have pleaded as his warrant. Germany, however, thought otherwise of the new tragedy than the serene critic of Würtemberg: it was performed with vast applause at the neighbouring city of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANNHEIM">Mannheim</a>; and thither, under a most excusable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in his own play, the young poet clandestinely went. On his return he was placed under <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>. And soon afterwards, being now thoroughly disgusted, and, with some reason, alarmed by the tyranny of the duke, Schiller finally eloped to Mannheim, availing himself of the confusion created in Stuttgart by the visit of a foreign prince. At Mannheim he lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Dalberg, a man of some rank and of sounding titles, but in Mannheim known chiefly as the literary manager (or what is called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>) of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. This connection aided in determining the subsequent direction of Schiller's talents; and his Fiesco, his Intrigue and Love, his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Carlos, and his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Stuart, followed within a short period of years. None of these are so far free from the faults of the Robbers as to merit a separate notice; for with less power, they are almost equally licentious. Finally, however, he brought out his Wallenstein, an immortal drama, and, beyond all competition, the nearest in point of excellence to the dramas of Shakspeare. The position of the characters of Max Piccolomini and the Princess Thekla is the finest instance of what, in a critical sense, is called relief, that literature offers. Young, innocent, unfortunate, among a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of ambitious, guilty, and bloodstained men, they offer a depth and solemnity of impression which is equally required by way of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> and of final repose. From Mannheim, where he had a transient love affair with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAURA">Laura</a> Dalberg, the daughter of his friend the director, Schiller removed to Jena, the celebrated university in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke of that German <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> was at this time gathering around him the most eminent of the German intellects; and he was eager to enrol Schiller in the body of his professors. In 1799 Schiller received the chair of civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and not long after he married Miss Longefeld, with whom he had been for some time acquainted. In 1803 he was ennobled; that is, he was raised to the rank of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, and entitled to attach the prefix of Von to his name. His income was now sufficient for domestic comfort and respectable independence; while in the society of Goethe, Herder, and other eminent wits, he found even more relaxation for his intellect, than his intellect, so fervent and so self-sustained, could require. Meantime the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of Schiller was gradually undermined; his lungs had been long subject to attacks of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; and the warning indications which constantly arose of some deep-seated organic injuries in his pulmonary system ought to have put him on his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> for some years before his death. Of all men, however, it is remarkable that Schiller was the most criminally negligent of his health; remarkable, we say, because for a period of four years Schiller had applied himself seriously to the study of medicine. The strong coffee, and the wine, which he drank, may not have been so injurious as his biographers suppose; but his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of sitting up through the night, and defrauding his wasted frame of all natural and restorative sleep, had something in it of that guilt which belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>. On the 9th of May 1805 his complaint reached its crisis. Early in the morning he became delirious; at noon his delirium abated; and at four in the afternoon he fell into a gentle unagitated sleep, from which he soon awoke. Conscious that he now stood on the very edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, he calmly and fervently took a last farewell of his friends. At six in the evening he fell again into sleep, from which, however, he again awoke once more to utter the memorable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, "that many things were growing plain and clear to his understanding." After this the cloud of sleep again settled upon him; a sleep which soon changed into the cloud of death. This event produced a profound impression throughout Germany. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> were closed at Weimar, and the funeral was conducted with public honours. The position in point of time, and the peculiar services of Schiller to the German literature, we have already stated: it remains to add, that in person he was tall, and of a strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> structure, but not muscular, and strikingly lean. His forehead was lofty, his nose aquiline, and his mouth almost of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. With other good points about his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and with auburn <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, it may be presumed that his whole appearance was pleasing and impressive; while in later years the character of sadness and contemplative sensibility deepened the impression of his countenance.
